item.title: Family Seeks Hate Crime Charge in Near-Fatal Attack on Somali Uber Driver
item.description:
Law enforcement officials in Minnesota announced on Monday that a suspect was in custody in connection with a weekend assault that left a Somali Uber driver in critical condition, an attack that the man’s family said was a hate crime.

The victim, Mohamed Yusuf, had picked up a passenger around 2 a.m. local time on Saturday when the man, who was riding from Minneapolis to Hopkins, Minn., a nearby suburb, became violent toward him, according to the authorities and Mr. Yusuf’s family.

Moments earlier, Mr. Yusuf’s attacker had asked him what his name was, and when he replied that it was Mohamed, the man voiced his anti-Muslim views, Osman Ahmed, Mr. Yusuf’s brother-in-law, said in an interview on Monday.

“‘I don’t like Mohamed,’” Mr. Ahmed said the man told his relative. “‘I don’t like that name.’”

The exchange was overheard by another family member who was speaking on the phone to Mr. Yusuf at the time of the attack, during which the passenger used Mr. Yusuf’s car to run over him, Mr. Ahmed said. Additional details about the attack were not immediately available from the police.

Mr. Yusuf, whom Mr. Ahmed said is in his 50s and is married with five children, was hospitalized at Hennepin County Medical Center in Minneapolis and was in a coma as of Monday afternoon, according to his family, which urged the authorities to treat the attack as a hate crime. Details about the assault emerged over the weekend on The Somali Brief, a news outlet that covers Somali-American news.

Law enforcement officials had not released the name of the suspect, who they said was being held on probable cause for assault but had not been formally charged.

“Investigators are examining all available evidence and considering all potential motives, including whether bias played a role in the assault,” Brent Johnson, the chief of the Hopkins Police Department, said in a statement. “Our responsibility is to follow the evidence, establish the facts and ensure that any criminal charges are supported by the investigation.”

In a statement on Monday, Mary Moriarty, the elected prosecutor in Hennepin County, said investigators were gathering evidence about the motivation behind the attack.

“In Minnesota, what are commonly referred to as ‘hate crimes’ are called ‘crimes motivated by bias,’” Ms. Moriarty said. “Prosecutors are required to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the crime was motivated by bias.”

A representative for Uber said on Monday that the ride-hailing company was cooperating with investigators and had offered its support to Mr. Yusuf’s family.

“We are shocked and horrified by the details of this senseless attack,” the company representative said. “We banned the rider from the Uber platform and are keeping the driver and his loved ones in our thoughts as we continue to support law enforcement with their investigation.”

Mr. Yusuf was born in Somalia and his family had recently moved from Rochester, Minn., to Blaine, Minn., which is about 17 miles north of Minneapolis, according to Mr. Ahmed, who said his brother-in-law was working full time driving for Uber.

Minnesota is home to the largest diaspora of Somalis in the United States, a community whose members began migrating to the state in large numbers as the East African nation descended into civil war in the mid-1990s.

That community has been the subject of repeated hostility from some Republicans, including President Trump and Representative Tom Emmer, Republican of Minnesota, the House whip, one of the top leaders in the caucus.

While appearing this month on the right-wing podcaster Benny Johnson’s show, Mr. Emmer said the migration of Somalis had brought violence to Minnesota.

“Well, I’ve got basically the Somali civil war that’s come to the state of Minnesota,” Mr. Emmer said.

During that podcast, Mr. Emmer assailed Representative Ilhan Omar, Democrat of Minnesota, who in 2018 became the first Somali-American elected to Congress and has been the target of a sprawling investigation by the Trump administration into her immigration history and financial dealings.

“She’s said in the past that she’s here to represent Somalia,” Mr. Emmer said. “Well, why don’t you go back to Somalia?”

A spokeswoman for Mr. Emmer did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.

In a social media post on Sunday, Ms. Omar condemned the assault, saying that the political environment had contributed to the situation.

“The relentless dehumanization of the Somali community has real consequences,” Ms. Omar wrote on X. “We must unequivocally condemn this violence and reject the hatred that divides our communities.”

Outside the hospital where Mr. Yusuf was being treated, a group of Somali-Americans gathered on Monday to draw attention to the attack. Among them was Zaynab Mohamed, a state senator from Minneapolis who was born in Somalia.

“I just have a quick question for the Somali people here: How many of you guys have Mohamed in your name or a family member who is named Mohamed?” she said. “Almost every single person. For a reason.”

item.title: Victim Advocates Sue Newsom Over Attempt to Empty California’s Death Row
item.description:
California prosecutors and the families of murder victims sued Gov. Gavin Newsom on Monday over his move to commute all death sentences in the state, saying that it amounts to an abuse of power that must be stopped.

The lawsuit asks the California Supreme Court to block Mr. Newsom’s mass commutation and allow time for each of the state’s 548 death sentences to be reviewed individually.

Earlier this month, Mr. Newsom said he felt a moral obligation to convert all death sentences to life in prison, though he acknowledged that his decision would “anger and hurt some Californians.”

The suit, filed by the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, a nonprofit group focused on victims’ rights, alleges that Mr. Newsom violated laws requiring that prosecutors and victims’ survivors have input on whether a prisoner’s sentence should be reduced. The plaintiffs also argue that there are errors in some inmates’ criminal records that raise questions about whether the governor has the legal authority to reduce certain sentences.

Under California law, a governor may unilaterally commute the sentence of a prisoner who is convicted of a felony in a single case. However, the governor must seek approval from the state Supreme Court to reduce the sentences of inmates with convictions in multiple felony cases.

Mr. Newsom has sent a list of 382 prisoners with multiple convictions to the state Supreme Court, seeking approval to commute their sentences. The rest of the death sentences were for prisoners convicted in single cases, according to Mr. Newsom, allowing him to reduce sentences unilaterally.

But the lawsuit says that some of the prisoners on Mr. Newsom’s list of people with a single conviction might actually have more felony convictions and cannot have their sentences reduced without court approval. The plaintiffs asked the court to stop Mr. Newsom from granting clemency until the cases could be thoroughly vetted.

Everyone on California’s death row has been convicted of murder — and many of them committed especially grisly crimes. Some are serial killers, while others have kidnapped and murdered young children.

Surviving family members of murder victims held dueling news conferences last week over Mr. Newsom’s commutations. One group said that it supported his decision and urged the court to move swiftly to approve commutations. The relatives said that executions would not help them heal from their losses and said they would rather see the justice system deliver more support for survivors of violence.

The other group expressed deep anguish at the notion that their loved ones’ killers could receive mercy. The relatives blasted Mr. Newsom for disrespecting them and said his actions had opened up old wounds, causing them to lose faith in the finality they had sought from the justice system.

Associations representing district attorneys, police officers and crime survivors said in the lawsuit that California law does not allow a blanket commutation like the one Mr. Newsom is seeking. They say that one person does not have the power to overrule the judgment of thousands of jurors and hundreds of judges in one fell swoop.

“A mass clemency is inconsistent with a scheme designed to create a public process that ensures that all relevant information is considered regarding the individual crime and criminal,” the lawsuit says.

Other lawyers have argued that the governor has broad authority to grant clemency and that he may empty death row based on his moral opposition to capital punishment, regardless of the details of each case.

Mr. Newsom has been a vocal opponent of the death penalty for decades. In announcing his decision to commute all death sentences in the state, the governor said that he was taking a “righteous action” based on his personal beliefs.

“I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing,” Mr. Newsom wrote in a letter announcing his decision.

He said that the state constitution provided governors with clemency powers “for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice.”

“For me, this is that moment,” he wrote.

Mr. Newsom’s request presents a novel situation for the state’s highest court.

When the court normally reviews a governor’s clemency request, it considers a specific prisoner’s fitness for clemency, including rehabilitation. This is the first time the California Supreme Court has been asked to approve hundreds of commutations at once based on a governor’s moral opposition to capital punishment, as opposed to the merits of an inmate’s specific circumstances.

The court has asked that opinions about Mr. Newsom’s commutation request be filed by Nov. 24. It must make a decision before he leaves office on Jan. 4.

item.title: Trump Administration Divide on China Policy Breaks Into Public View
item.description:
President Trump headed on Monday for a trip to Asia to meet President Xi Jinping of China with his administration openly divided over how hard to squeeze that country on artificial intelligence technology, as he noted that he has not wanted to make moves that “insult China.”

The public airing of the fight over China policy inside Mr. Trump’s cabinet shows how much the fallout of the Nvidia scandal has deepened fissures inside the government, forcing into view a debate about how the United States should reckon with Beijing.

Mr. Trump, who is due to meet Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia at a summit in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen this week, has struggled to balance national security concerns about America’s most powerful rival against his desire to prop up Nvidia’s chips business and avoid another trade war with Mr. Xi.

Those tensions were center stage on Monday as the president acknowledged that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had been at odds over how hard to crack down on a loophole that has allowed China to access advanced A.I. chips through data centers in other countries.

“One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China,” Mr. Trump said of his two cabinet secretaries, speaking to reporters on the South Lawn before leaving for Asia. “Both are acceptable, but they’re different views.”

The debate intensified with the resignation last week of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, after revelations that he had two extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a woman whom U.S. officials have identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

Amid the fallout, Mr. Trump has appeared more concerned in public about offending Mr. Xi than about the risks to national security. He has downplayed reports about the warnings he received from U.S. intelligence officials and Secretary of State Marco Rubio personally about Mr. Huang’s relationship and the spying by China.

Chinese officials have denied that Ms. Huang is an intelligence operative. And on Monday, Mr. Trump again cast doubt on it.

“I don’t know that she is a spy,” he told reporters. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy.”

A reporter noted that Mr. Rubio had warned him about Ms. Huang being spy. “Who told me that?” the president asked.

Told that it was Mr. Rubio, he said: “I haven’t heard that.”

When asked where the president stood in the debate about how to approach China, a White House spokesman, Matthew Middleton, touted the new rule the administration issued on Monday to close the loophole giving China access to advanced American chips through third countries.

“This action will help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to U.S. S.I. innovators, not Chinese shell companies,” he said in a statement, a reference to Mr. Trump’s preferred term of “super intelligence.”

“The Trump administration will continue to take decisive action to protect America’s technological edge, strengthen our national security and ensure the future of S.I. is built in America,” Mr. Middleton added.

The divide over China policy inside the Trump administration goes beyond the two feuding cabinet secretaries, according to more than half a dozen current and former officials with direct knowledge of the discussions. On one side of the fight is Mr. Lutnick, whose department writes and enforces chip export rules and who pushed for a softer version of the restrictions on data centers. On the other side are Mr. Bessent; Mr. Rubio, who is also Mr. Trump’s national security adviser; the U.S. trade representative, Jamieson Greer; and much of the National Security Council staff. All of them have pressed for months for broad limits on China’s access to A.I. chips.

The president has drifted between the two camps in private, depending on the day, according to advisers.

In a Friday television interview, Mr. Bessent faulted the Commerce Department for failing to sanction Megaspeed, the Singaporean company at the center of the Nvidia scandal, saying that the department “has the pen.” He also said that Nvidia should be “held accountable” if it did not do enough to stop the illegal diversion of chips to China.

On paper, Mr. Trump sided with his Treasury secretary. Shortly before he left for Asia, his administration issued the restrictions on China’s chip access that Mr. Bessent had pushed and that Mr. Lutnick had resisted.

But the president’s wavering comments on Monday left some China hawks inside and outside the administration worried that he might reverse himself or treat the new rule as a bargaining asset to trade with Mr. Xi.

When reporters asked the president about the delicate situation on Monday, he insisted that Mr. Lutnick was “doing a very good job.” He suggested that any delay in acting against Megaspeed had been meant to avoid upsetting Mr. Xi.

“If you didn’t delay it, if you didn’t do something, you could have a blowup with China,” Mr. Trump said. He added: “I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there.”

The new rule, issued by the Commerce Department on Monday morning, will require data centers outside the United States to get a government license before selling significant computing power to firms with headquarters in China, Russia, Iran and a small group of other high-risk countries. Officials say that will close a loophole that has let Chinese firms rent the advanced Nvidia chips they are barred from buying, access that has helped China’s A.I. industry advance rapidly. U.S. officials involved in the debate have said that China’s A.I. models pose a major threat of cyberattacks against the United States.

The news release announcing the move carried an unusual line that reflected the fight behind it: The rule, the Commerce Department said, had been “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council.”

The new policy takes effect in 90 days. Enforcing it will fall to Mr. Lutnick, a staunch opponent of the measure. A person close to Mr. Lutnick said he had repeatedly warned the president and his colleagues that the restrictions could start another trade war with China. Another person close to Mr. Lutnick said the disclaimer about the Treasury Department and the N.S.C. was meant to make clear who was responsible for what they view as a misguided policy.

The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive last week under pressure from the company’s board, after revelations about his relationships with a company executive and Ms. Huang, whom U.S. officials have identified as an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Ms. Huang founded Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center company that U.S. authorities are investigating over allegations of smuggling chips to China. (Megaspeed has said that it operates a lawful and legitimate business.)

The Times has previously reported that Mr. Trump was warned at least twice about Mr. Huang’s relationship, late last year and again in the spring. According to two U.S. officials briefed on the matter, Mr. Rubio was so concerned about Mr. Huang’s entanglement with Ms. Huang that he wrote a classified memo on March 30 summarizing intelligence that showed she was in contact with China’s top spy agency. Then in May, aboard Air Force One, Mr. Rubio briefed Mr. Trump on the intelligence in person, the officials said.

The secret intelligence about Ms. Huang played a backstage role in shaping the president’s trip to Beijing in May, the officials said. Mr. Huang was left off the initial list of executives invited. But after news reports noted his absence, Mr. Trump called him, and Mr. Huang traveled to Anchorage to meet Air Force One at its scheduled stopover. At the time, Mr. Trump called reports that Mr. Huang had not been invited “FAKE NEWS!”

Mr. Trump has stood by Mr. Huang throughout the saga. Last week, The Times has reported, the president called him and urged him to fight for his job. On Monday, the president said he “would not mind” seeing Mr. Huang reinstated. “I think he learned a big lesson,” Mr. Trump said.

Mr. Huang has cultivated the president since the start of the second term, praising him lavishly in public and making announcements of huge investments that Mr. Trump has touted as administration successes.

In August 2025, Mr. Trump allowed Nvidia to resume exports of its H20 chips to China on condition of a 15 percent cut for the government — though Beijing never approved the sales. Two months later, Nvidia committed $25 million to Mr. Trump’s White House ballroom.

In December, Mr. Trump announced that Nvidia could sell its more powerful H200 chips to China in exchange for 25 percent of revenue flowing to the U.S. government. Mr. Trump has told aides he regards Nvidia as central to the stock market and the broader economy.

The data center rule had stalled within the administration for months. Mr. Trump approved it in August, according to two senior officials, but the Commerce Department did not issue it. The Biden administration had imposed similar restrictions just before leaving office. The Trump administration rescinded them last year, and several drafts of replacement rules have died since.

Current and former officials who support a tougher stance against Beijing said they hoped that Mr. Trump’s words on Monday were merely diplomatic niceties, and that he would follow through on the chip restrictions and let the Megaspeed investigation run its course.

Others who have worked for the president were more skeptical. Since Mr. Trump retreated from his tariff war with Beijing in May 2025, he has made clear to his national security team that he is wary of taking any actions that might disrupt the trading relationship.

H.R. McMaster, who served as Mr. Trump’s national security adviser in 2017 and 2018 and has been critical of the president since leaving the administration, said Mr. Trump’s instinct for deal-making had repeatedly undercut his China policy.

“I think President Trump is often impeded by his belief that he can get the deal nobody else can get,” Mr. McMaster said. “And as a result, instead of having a consistent policy of competing against China’s policy of economic aggression, he often vacillates and weakens his own position.”

item.title: These Newborns Are the Size of Strawberries and Already Crawling
item.description:
In the middle of the night on a beach in Southern California, 54 newborn sea turtles scuttled onto the sand and made history.

The hatchlings, each roughly the size of a large strawberry and not weighing much more, are the first ever known to be born in California, emerging from eggs laid in September in Seal Beach, about 30 miles south of downtown Los Angeles.

They are known as olive ridley sea turtles, a protected species most commonly found in tropical and subtropical waters off the coasts of Mexico and India. Experts say that unusually temperate ocean waters tied to a major El Niño — a recurring climate pattern characterized by warmer Pacific Ocean temperatures — appear to have drawn the creatures to the shores of California.

Olive ridley sea turtles can live for 50 years and are the smallest type of sea turtle, weighing up to 100 pounds and measuring about three feet in length.

A few days after the Seal Beach nest was discovered in September, another was spotted a few miles south, near the Huntington Pier. Biologists say that a different mother turtle laid each of the nests, both in Orange County.

Scientists soon moved the clutches to the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach to keep them safe from high tides and flooding, and to control the temperature and humidity as the eggs incubated for up to two months. There were concerns that the nighttime temperatures in California would be too cold for the eggs, which typically don’t do well below 80 degrees Fahrenheit.

A third sea turtle nest found in November in Ventura, about 100 miles north, was destroyed by high tides, said Jonathan Snyder, a biologist with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

In total, the two nests from Orange County contained 204 eggs, said Lance Adams, the director of veterinary services at the Aquarium of the Pacific. As of Monday afternoon, 94 had hatched and been released, he said, and staff members were monitoring the remaining eggs to see how many more would end up being viable.

Dr. Adams said he had feared that none of the eggs would hatch. So it was a delight to see the first baby emerge on Friday night from beneath the sand lining the aquarium’s incubator. Within hours, dozens more had hatched, in what Dr. Adams called ”an eruption of baby sea turtles.”

“That was a big relief,” he said in an interview on Monday.

Scientists think the mother turtles came from Mexico, their closest breeding grounds, but they plan to test DNA from shell fragments to identify which colonies the mothers belonged to.

Cali Turner Tomaszewicz, a research biologist with the National Marine Fisheries Service, the federal agency charged with protecting marine life, said it was common for Californians to spot olive ridleys in the open ocean, while on a fishing or whale watching boat. But it had been rare to see them near the beach — until this year.

“We’ve gotten a lot of reports of olive ridleys near shore, all up and down the coast, from San Diego all the way up through Monterey Bay this year,” Dr. Tomaszewicz said at a news briefing over the weekend.

The baby turtles have a big challenge ahead of them, Dr. Adams said. Once they enter the sea waters, they must swim for days and make it past fish and other predators until they reach the open ocean. Scientists estimate that only one in a thousand olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings reach adulthood, which is about 10 to 15 years old.

For those that do mature, many will try to return to the Orange County beaches from where they were released to lay their eggs — if the ocean cooperates, Dr. Adams said.

“If it’s cold here they’re not going to come here, they’re going to stay in the warm water,” he said.

item.title: Justice Alito Warns Court Overhaul Could Threaten Judicial Independence
item.description:
Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. on Monday warned against proposals to overhaul the Supreme Court by altering its composition, a move that he said would threaten the judiciary’s traditional independence.

His remarks came as Democrats, many of whom have advocated changes to the court, including expanding its membership or adopting term limits for the justices, prepare to take control of Congress in January.

Justice Alito did not detail any specific legislative proposal or refer to the change in political control on the horizon. However, speaking during a black-tie dinner in his honor hosted by the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank, he pointedly critiqued the court’s critics, wading into the public debate over the justices’ rulings.

He described what he characterized as a mounting campaign in recent years by those opposed to the court’s rulings to change the direction of its decisions by intimidating and harassing justices.

“Or,” he said, “if that fails, by seriously damaging the court’s standing in the eyes of the public, and then altering the court’s composition,” he said.

“If that campaign succeeds, the Supreme Court as an institution will be fundamentally changed, and perhaps permanently,” he told the hundreds of people gathered at the ornate National Building Museum.

The court, Justice Alito said, could “soon face a structural question of greater magnitude: whether the court will be allowed to continue as an independent tribunal that decides cases based on its understanding of the law, not political pressure.”

In recent years, the Supreme Court’s conservative majority has overturned longstanding precedent, ending race-conscious policies in college admissions, eliminating the nationwide right to abortion and limiting the power of federal agencies.

In 2022, Justice Alito wrote the decision reversing Roe v. Wade and overturning the constitutional right to abortion.

Recent polls have shown declining public opinion of the Supreme Court, with a majority of Americans saying the justices are motivated mainly by politics rather than law, according to a September survey conducted by Marquette University Law School.

As poll numbers have dropped, elected leaders and newly elected Democrats in Congress have called for an overhaul of the court. Such proposals in the past have included expanding the size of the court, ending life tenure for justices and strengthening ethics policies for the justices.

Following the court’s decision last term to significantly weaken the landmark Voting Rights Act, members of the Congressional Black Caucus, for instance, said they would work to “aggressively advance Supreme Court reform. We will work to establish term limits for justices to help restore independence, neutrality and legitimacy to the court.”

In a letter this month seeking support for his candidacy for House speaker, Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York, said lawmakers must “clean up the mess at the Supreme Court.”

While polls have shown that Democrats have been particularly upset with the court’s decisions, displeasure has also been rising among Republicans. President Trump has been particularly vocal and personal in his criticism, especially when any of the three justices he nominated to the bench have ruled against him.

Along with Justice Clarence Thomas, Justice Alito has emerged as the member of the court most likely to side with Mr. Trump’s policies. Speculation had mounted following the midterm election that he might retire to allow Mr. Trump to name his replacement before Democrats take control of the Senate in January.

He has told people close to him, however, that he has no intention of announcing his retirement and plans to remain on the bench at least through the conclusion of the court’s current term next summer.

In his remarks on Monday, Justice Alito described the judiciary as the weakest of the three branches of government and said its independence ultimately depended on “the sufferance of the other more powerful branches.”

“What may matter most in the end,” he added, “is popular support for an independent judiciary.”

item.title: An Artist Nearly Died in a Crash. Strangers Helped Him Draw Again.
item.description:
It was a Sunday night, and Paul Madonna was driving home on a dark road through John McLaren Park in San Francisco. He crested a hill, and his whole life changed.

His last memories from Nov. 6, 2022, are of a pair of bright headlights zooming straight at him — in his lane. The sound of crunching metal. Then, blackness.

Mr. Madonna woke up four days later in a hospital bed. He looked down to see large staples holding together each side of a long incision stretching down his torso. He saw a web of tubes connected to his body and a machine helping him breathe.

“Something terrible has happened to me,” he thought.

Mr. Madonna was famous for his highly realistic, extremely detailed drawings of San Francisco. He had sketched the city’s landmarks, including its Victorian homes, towers, parks and hillside staircases, for “All Over Coffee,” his strip in the San Francisco Chronicle that ran for 12 years. He produced several popular books.

But the crash wrecked him. He suddenly had a brain injury, a torn carotid artery, a broken nose, nerve pain and a right foot that, as doctors described, was like “a bag of broken cornflakes,” he said. The impact pushed his stomach into his diaphragm and other organs into his lungs.

Miraculously, one of the few body parts left unscathed was his right hand.

He was bedridden for the first six months after the crash, sleeping as many as 23 hours a day, and his hand-eye coordination was all out of whack. His first drawing after the crash, dated March 17, 2023, was a self-portrait. It looks almost child-like, a mix of squiggly lines that only somewhat resembles a face.

“It’s hard when you know you’re better at something than you’re doing at the moment,” he said.

Over the past four years, Mr. Madonna, 54, found a touch of the divine in the kindness of strangers. They came in response to a plea that he posted on social media for someone, anyone, to come to his home to sit for a portrait.

The artist knew he needed to retrain himself, but he could not yet roam the city in search of his usual subject matter. He asked his visitors to sit for free, and he would draw their portraits. But the results, he warned, could be dreadful.

More than 100 people, most of them strangers, signed up, and a new person arrived every few days.

The sessions were meant to give Mr. Madonna different subjects so that he could teach himself how to draw again. But they also became mini-support groups as the artist told the visitors about his crash, over and over again.

Now, he has recovered enough to have his first art show since the crash: “We Came Here to See,” at the Nelson Duni gallery in San Francisco through Dec. 3. And the portraits he drew during those visits comprise part of the exhibition.

“I used the creative process to literally bring myself back to life,” he said in an interview.

Ken Newman, a songwriter and guitarist, was among those who signed up to be sketched by him.

“I didn’t know the guy at all,” Mr. Newman recalled. “I just knew him by reputation.”

Mr. Newman said he had been feeling frustrated about hitting age 72, with his aches and pains and the realization that most of his life was behind him. But as he strummed his guitar and Mr. Madonna drew him, the men talked about the crash and life in general. They cried together. Mr. Newman said it helped him put his own aging in perspective.

“Most of my tears were empathetic, like I can’t imagine what that would have been like,” Mr. Newman said. “Paul was really opening up. I don’t remember the context, but I do remember how I felt. Like it was a gift we gave to each other.”

Another visitor was Joseph Amster, who leads walking tours in the city dressed as Emperor Norton, an eccentric San Franciscan who in 1859 had pronounced himself “Norton I, Emperor of the United States.”

For the sitting, Mr. Amster dressed in full regalia, with medallions hanging from his chest and red and purple feathers adorning his top hat.

Back then, he said, Mr. Madonna was thin and haggard and got around the studio with the help of a knee scooter.

Mr. Amster’s husband, Rick Shelton, also posed for a portrait. He recalled Mr. Madonna saying that if his artery had been nicked a tiny bit more — the width of a paper cut — he would have died.

“It’s a reminder of how fragile we all are,” Mr. Shelton said.

Slowly, Mr. Madonna’s skills came back. His portraits grew more detailed and realistic, like his prior sketches of the city. After the current exhibition ends, he said, he will give those portraits to the people who sat for him as a thank you.

His art has progressed far faster than the case against the man who has been accused of hitting him. According to the San Francisco police officers who responded to the crash scene, the driver of a black Mercedes-Benz sedan had been speeding and crossed a double yellow line before plowing into Mr. Madonna’s car. The Mercedes was unregistered and uninsured, the police said.

Witnesses said they saw the driver of the Mercedes flee the vehicle. The police found a package in the car addressed to Eduardo Sanchez Giron, 35, and went to the address listed on the mailing label. Mr. Giron’s brother said that Mr. Giron had told him he had been involved in a crash, the police said, and Mr. Giron was arrested and released on bail.

Brooke Jenkins, the San Francisco district attorney, has charged Mr. Giron with felony hit and run causing great bodily injury.

Mr. Madonna said that he has appeared in court 29 times since the crash, but no trial date has yet been set. Mr. Giron is due back in court on Friday.

The San Francisco Public Defender’s office, which is representing Mr. Giron, declined to discuss him or the circumstances of the crash. Attempts to reach Mr. Giron were unsuccessful.

The San Francisco criminal justice system has always moved slowly, but the courts have faced additional backlogs in recent years because of shutdowns during the Covid-19 pandemic and more cases being filed by Ms. Jenkins than by her predecessor. Court staff went on strike briefly this year, saying they were overburdened.

Mr. Madonna said the past four years have been the most humbling ones of his life. He learned that the criminal justice system does not move like an episode of “Law and Order” and is filled with delays and aggravation.

Though he is angry about the case, he has learned to be gentle with himself. He went from being a 50-year-old at the top of his game, he said, to feeling like an old man, less fit, much grayer and walking with a cane. A young woman called him an elder the other day, and it stung a little.

Once a bike messenger who could whip through the city’s chaotic streets, Mr. Madonna is now scared to cross the road, fearful that he may not make it before the light turns red.

He has constant pain in his right foot. He needs naps. He used to love having a busy schedule, but if he traipses around the city one day, he needs to rest the next.

Still, he is alive. He is making art again. Hundreds of people have come to his show, and some of his work has sold.

And that, for now, is enough.

item.title: Measles Is Officially Back in the United States. What Now?
item.description:
The United States has returned to a time, until recently unimaginable, when measles is a persistent threat, not just a sporadic one that can easily be snuffed out.

Even with rigorous effort, it is likely to take years to regain measles elimination status, which the country officially lost on Tuesday. By Blacki Migliozzi/The New York Times

Local and state health departments will need more resources to combat outbreaks. Doctors, parents and teachers will need to familiarize themselves with the symptoms, and prepare to quarantine anyone who is unvaccinated and exposed for 21 days. Hospitals will need to prepare for an onslaught of patients infected with a highly contagious virus. Public health officials may need new tools to detect, diagnose and stem outbreaks quickly. And they may need to revise the recommended vaccination schedule to protect the most vulnerable.

“We’re really in kind of a new Wild West of our own making,” said Dr. Christopher Monson, an intensive care pediatrician at the University of Rochester.

“Lots of people are going to get sick, and some people are going to die,” he added. “It’s just sad that we’re spending this much energy on things we had already fixed.”

Measles is among the most contagious viruses known. It lingers in the air for hours and infects nine of every 10 unprotected people who are exposed to it. The illness begins with typical respiratory symptoms, such as a runny nose and cough, then rapidly progresses to characteristic white spots inside the mouth and a rash that spreads down from the hairline to the feet. In some people, the virus may also ravage the lungs, the brain and other organs.

About 11 percent of measles patients in the United States this year were hospitalized, and 10 people have died.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention did not provide responses to questions about its plans to prepare for and address measles outbreaks.

In recent months, the C.D.C. gave states a surprise infusion of $100 million to bolster immunization efforts and improve surveillance of the disease. But that may not be enough.

The costs for immunization drives, case investigation, contact tracing and quarantine can quickly add up. It took $8.7 million to stamp out an outbreak that started at a migrant shelter in Chicago in 2024 and $5.4 million to control a 2025 cluster in New Mexico.

Measles cases dropped precipitously after the arrival of the vaccine in 1963. The introduction of a second dose, in 1989, helped the country eliminate the threat. Declining vaccination rates are the main reason the measles virus has reclaimed a foothold in the United States.

Regaining elimination status will require bringing them back up to 95 percent, a threshold known as herd immunity, to keep the virus from spreading in communities, medical experts said.

Five of the 10 deaths were in children too young to be vaccinated. The remaining were in unvaccinated adults, who might have previously been shielded by herd immunity. “Completely unvaccinated adults getting measles — I mean that’s going to take us back 30, 40 years,” said Dr. David Hamer, an infectious diseases physician at Boston University.

The number of cases this year has topped 5,400, more than double last year’s tally and the highest since 1991, nearly a decade before the country attained elimination status. About 96 percent of the known cases this year have been in those who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown.

“I have no confidence to think 2027 will be even better,” said Dr. Scott Roberts, an infectious disease doctor at Yale New Haven Health. “I mean, at this rate, it’s looking to be exponentially worse.”

Infection with measles erases the body’s immune memory, leaving patients newly vulnerable even to diseases they already had. It can also cause long-term complications in some people, including subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a fatal neurological condition that can develop years after the initial illness.

“It’s really a bad disease and dangerous, and I think people need to appreciate that,” Dr. Hamer said.

The first dose of the combined measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is typically given at 12 months. But that schedule is devised for a country with low risk of exposure to measles.

“At what point would we modify the vaccine schedule to address this increasing risk?” said Dr. Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University.

Some experts now recommend vaccinating young babies before travel to outbreak areas within the United States. As measles becomes more common, the guidance may need to expand to include all infants, Dr. Lo said.

That approach is also complicated, however. Giving the first dose at 6 months is thought to blunt the vaccine’s effectiveness long term. In many parts of the world where measles is endemic — a constant and predictable presence — the first dose is instead routinely given at 9 months, Dr. Lo said. Officials may also need to consider a second dose for adults who received only a single shot when they were children.

Some states are already trying multiple approaches to increase immunization rates. In Delaware, the state health department has set up mobile vaccination units in the parking lots of local businesses and extended hours at public health clinics. New Jersey has purchased billboards urging people to get vaccinated and hosted immunization drives at schools and community events. New York declared a statewide health emergency over measles, allowing retired doctors, nurses and pharmacists to administer shots.

Decades of studies have shown that the measles vaccine is safe. But messaging urging vaccination has sometimes been too forceful and too dismissive of parents’ concerns about safety, said Mary Politi, a co-director of the Center for Collaborative Care Decisions at Washington University in St. Louis.

People “need more accessible information with stories and relatable experiences, so that they don’t feel like they’ll be cast aside if they ask a question,” she added.

To stamp out outbreaks, public health officials will need to detect them early, before the virus has had a chance to circulate widely.

At the population level, wastewater surveillance can indicate where measles may be percolating, long before a patient seeks medical care.

Measles “is such an infectious virus that people excrete a lot of it, so just one person in the sewer shed can excrete enough into wastewater that it lights up,” said Alexandria Boehm, a researcher at WastewaterSCAN, an academic initiative that includes 150 wastewater treatment plants.

Wastewater monitoring in Houston picked up genetic material from the measles virus on Jan. 7, 2025, two weeks before the first case in the state was confirmed. In Oregon, wastewater testing detected measles 10 weeks before the first case was reported in June 2024. Officials in those communities alerted doctors and public health officials.

The C.D.C. set up the National Wastewater Surveillance System during the Covid pandemic and expanded it to include 1,500 sites, covering nearly half the country’s population. That emergency funding expired at the end of September.

The Trump administration has proposed cutting the program’s budget to about $25 million a year from $125 million.

As measles cases continue to rise, federal agencies must also contend with the need to test, isolate and treat patients quickly, said Alexander Greninger, a virologist at the University of Washington in Seattle.

Doctors who suspect measles in a patient must first request a test from a public health clinic. That process can take several hours, and a result may take two to five days, or longer in some states.

What is needed instead is a commercial test that can be run at any lab or hospital, preferably made by a manufacturer whose machines are already in wide use, Dr. Greninger said. The first-ever rapid test for measles, which would enable testing at any doctor’s office, will soon be rolled out in some low-income countries.

If a global company were to invest in a measles test and get it approved by the Food and Drug Administration, the test could be used all over the world, he added: “That’s the real game changer here.” (Dr. Greninger helps many such companies generate data for regulatory approval.)

The elimination of measles in the United States has meant that few American doctors practicing today have had experience with the disease.

“We know what to do about measles — how it spreads, what type of isolation you need, how to clean the environment,” said Dr. Marci Drees, the chief infection prevention officer at ChristianaCare, a health system in Delaware. But, she added, “we just haven’t had to do it in so long that it feels very new for people.”

Some hospitals are conducting drills to train staff members to identify measles symptoms and quickly isolate patients before they put others at risk.

Dr. Monson, the intensive care pediatrician, had never seen a measles case until last month, when he treated two school-age siblings who were hospitalized for weeks. To safely transport the patients, the Rochester hospital cleared hallways and blocked off elevators for periods. Even after the children were isolated, staff members worried about the other critically ill patients who might be exposed to the virus by the nurses or respiratory therapists attending to the children.

Having never treated severely sick children with measles, the doctors were also stumped on treatment. Scientific papers on the subject date back to the 1960s and ’70s, so “none of the data is relevant to here and now and where we are,” Dr. Monson said.

The children were intubated for longer and needed more oxygen than doctors had anticipated, for example. Doctors in the United States will also need to learn how to treat adults who might become severely ill.

There is no specific treatment for measles, although some are being developed. Doctors primarily rely on antiviral drugs and supportive care.

The American Academy of Pediatrics and other professional organizations have put together some materials to help clinicians recognize, contain and treat measles.

The C.D.C. has a measles tool kit for public health departments but in terms of clinical guidance, “they are not helping as much as they should,” Dr. Monson said, adding, “Yet another area where we’re not seeing the support we used to have from our federal colleagues.”

item.title: Schools Are Closing Nationwide as Enrollment Drops. Parents Are Livid.
item.description:
The families show up angry and organized, wearing matching T-shirts and waving protest signs to vent their frustration at a crisis that has largely slipped under America’s political radar: Scores of neighborhood schools are closing.

Since last year, more than 100 public schools across the country have been slated for closure or consolidation, as districts grapple with dramatic enrollment declines that have led to strained budgets and half-empty buildings.

They are the first in a wave of school closures that is expected to accelerate in the years ahead as Americans have fewer and fewer children.

The issue got scant attention during the midterm elections compared with gas prices or the war in Iran. But it has become a personal, consuming fight for thousands of parents, liberal and conservative alike, who have thronged school-board meetings and formed grass-roots groups to argue that closures will scatter students and devastate neighborhoods anchored by local schools.

“It feels like our community is being dismantled,” said Hanna Neuschwander, who bikes her third grader and seventh grader to their neighborhood school in Portland, Ore., where 10 schools are being recommended for closure and others are being broken up and reconfigured.

Almost no type of district — urban or rural, affluent or poor — is immune. Pittsburgh is preparing to close 12 schools, and Tulsa, Okla. recently voted to close or consolidate 17. Five are closing around Tampa Bay, Fla., and three in Little Rock, Ark. In Colorado, schools are shuttering in the rich college town of Boulder and next to a mobile-home park outside Denver.

In New York City, the nation’s largest school district, enrollment has plunged from nearly 1 million to about 767,000 students over the last decade. Two small schools in Harlem are now on the potential closure list, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani is facing pressure to find solutions to a growing crisis.

Public-school enrollment is being battered on multiple fronts.

Americans worried about soaring prices and pessimistic about the future are having fewer children or forgoing parenthood altogether, and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has meant fewer immigrants are arriving and enrolling their children in public schools.

Public-school enrollment never fully recovered after plunging during the pandemic, and it is also facing pressure as more parents opt for charter schools, home-schooling or voucher-funded private schools.

“It was hard, but it was also necessary,” said Lori Goldstein, who as president of the Adams 12 school district in suburban Denver recently voted to close one middle school and five elementary schools. “People just aren’t having kids. Every year, our kindergarten class is getting smaller and smaller.”

In most cases, districts receive state and federal funding based on the number of students enrolled. Fewer students, districts say, means less money to pay for rigorous academic options, like advanced math, and a full slate of electives, like music, art and STEM, at every school — something districts hope to change by consolidating buildings.

Closures are a “last resort,” said Angela King Smith, a partner at Education Resource Strategies, a nonprofit that consults with school districts on finances. Districts typically start with smaller changes, like adjusting school boundaries or trying to woo new families — by expanding preschool or offering specialized programming, for example.

But “if those things are just not working,” she said, “it’s like, ‘Look, you’ve got to do something.’”

Often, schools in poorer neighborhoods struggle the most to fill classrooms and keep a full slate of options.

In Portland, enrollment has fallen from a peak of nearly 80,000 students in the 1960s to 42,000 today. The district says it has tried spreading music and art teachers out across schools, and it has increased high school class sizes to pay for counselors in some elementary schools. Still, about half of Portland’s students — and even fewer of its students in poverty — are in what the district considers a “sustainable school.”

“How are we going to achieve better for our kids if we maintain the status quo?” said Rashelle Chase-Miller, a Portland board member who believes closing some schools will help the district better serve its most vulnerable students.

For many families, the closures are a gut punch, injecting chaos and disruption to their children’s lives.

Parents are organizing on WhatsApp and Facebook, showing up to school-board meetings in their schools’ colors, and even going to court to try to block closures.

The plan in Portland has been particularly contentious. At a packed board meeting last month, parents and community members shoved past security, shouting “Shame on you!” and “Save our schools!” according to video posted by The Oregonian.

The superintendent, Kimberlee Armstrong, has faced accusations from teachers, parents and local Democratic Socialists of America organizers that she is part of a “right wing” effort to privatize education and hurt public schools.

Dr. Armstrong said in an interview that she was recommending closures as part of her commitment to all Portland students and the “long term stability” of the school system. “That is my job,” she said.

Some parents in Portland said they understood the need for changes but wanted the district to slow down and consider community input. “It’s not about ‘don’t close schools,’ but close schools the right way,” said Matt Coolidge, a parent who co-founded a grass-roots group, Save PDX Schools.

In Fort Collins, Colo., dozens of parents and students gathered outside the offices of the Poudre School District on a recent evening to urge the board to spare their schools.

For some of them, this was their first time joining a protest. But they wanted to come out for their schools and children.

“We’ve never been out to a protest before,” said Shelley Sutton, who brought her three young children to to the rally to save Timnath Elementary, home of the Cubs, one of five schools set to be closed.

The district said Timnath’s yellow-brick building — first built in 1919 — did not comply with the Americans With Disabilities Act and needed millions of dollars in upgrades.

But the Suttons said having Timnath in the neighborhood allowed them to walk their third-grader to school. If it closes, they said, many students will have to cross busy roads or an interstate to get to the closest school, making walking or biking dangerous.

“The school is the linchpin in the heart of town,” Ms. Sutton’s husband, Ian, said. “It’s the heart of the community.”

The district’s superintendent, Brian Kingsley, said more closures could loom if the student population continues to fall.

“This problem is not going to go away,” he said in an interview. “Nobody’s being asked to like these decisions, but it’s not the result of a local failure. Birthrates are lower. Fewer families are moving here.”

Some parents say that school boards are closing the wrong schools and putting unfair burdens on rural, immigrant or minority students.

In Minneapolis, a proposal to close up to 16 schools was criticized, in part, for including several schools in predominantly Black, working class neighborhoods.

“I hear parents say they feel angry. I hear parents say the trust in the district is lost,” said Shakiya Carter, a co-founder of Minneapolis Families for Public Schools, which opposed the plan and won a pause while the district considers its options.

Nationally, research shows that high-poverty schools and majority Black schools are more likely to be closed, even when accounting for similar enrollment declines.

Studies have found that closures can hurt students academically and may not save money, often because districts try to avoid laying off teachers and staff, the biggest line item on any district budget. The uncertainty can also spur families to look elsewhere — to private schools, charter schools or other districts — leading to new financial losses.

In Pittsburgh, a closure plan isn’t expected to be a huge cost saver, but the district hopes it will equalize resources.

At Arsenal Middle School, which serves mostly lower-income Black and Hispanic families in the gentrifying neighborhood of Lawrenceville, the student body has shrunk to 134 students, with just 37 eighth graders. That’s too few to offer 8th grade algebra, a pathway to higher level math that is available at some more affluent schools in the district.

With an influx of students from other middle schools, Arsenal hopes to offer algebra next year. David Saylor, a math teacher, said he has students who are ready to take it and that “parents absolutely love an advanced option.”

But as part of the plan, the elementary school on the other side of the building, Arsenal PreK-5, is closing. That will break up a tight-knit school community made up of many immigrant families.

The principal, Ruthie Rea, has been there 18 years, long enough to watch entire families of children come through the school. Next year, her students — her “Arsenal All Stars,” with their names on their lockers, and teachers who greet them with hugs — will be split among three different schools.

“I’m not letting my mind get there,” said Dr. Rea, who was awaiting word about where she and her staff will be reassigned. “We want this last year to be one that is super special.”

item.title: Classified N.S.A. Network Goes Down, Causing Work Disruptions
item.description:
The National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network was offline Tuesday, prompting the spy agency to tell its work force to stagger arrivals at its Maryland headquarters, according to people familiar with the matter.

The network, known as NSANet, is central to the agency’s work, according to current and former intelligence officials. It is used to send and receive top secret information. Much of the work that the agency conducts — including surveilling foreign spies and terrorists — is classified, so a disruption of the network would be a severe impediment.

There are currently no signs that the outage is the result of a cyberattack or other nefarious activity, the people said. NSANet has been unstable for weeks, one of the people said, which has fueled frustration within the work force. CNN reported the outage earlier.

A voice mail call box for National Security Agency employees reached by a New York Times reporter on Tuesday morning referred to the disruption as a “code yellow” for the spy agency’s Maryland day shift, the second-highest warning in a three-tier system.

“Nonemergency personnel should begin staggered arrival no earlier than noon,” the recording said. “Emergency personnel to report for duty as scheduled.”

The N.S.A. did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Based at Fort Meade, Md., the National Security Agency is one of the largest intelligence agencies in the U.S. government, with a work force of tens of thousands. It is the lead spy agency responsible for collecting signals intelligence, or electronic intercepts, of foreign communications for U.S. policymakers, and it plays a central role in overseeing the cybersecurity of government networks.

The disruption is the latest in a cascade of recent technology failures that have grabbed headlines in recent days, including a nationwide grounding of flights, an outage of Microsoft products and interruptions to banking services. None of those episodes have been linked to a cyberattack and have instead been blamed on routine technology issues.

item.title: Duffy Details Request for $50 Billion for Air Traffic Improvements
item.description:
The Trump administration on Tuesday laid out its rationale for requesting an additional $50.1 billion to fully modernize the air traffic control system, but the scant details are unlikely to satisfy skeptics in Congress.

Under the request from Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, $10.1 billion would go toward air traffic equipment modernization, including $2 billion for cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications. The rest would be used for airport infrastructure, replacement of terminals, and upgrading and building air traffic control centers and towers.

The explanation was included in a one-page letter to Senate and House Appropriations Committee leaders and signed by Mr. Duffy, Administrator Bryan Bedford of the Federal Aviation Administration and Russell T. Vought, director of the Office of Management and Budget.

Mr. Duffy was expected to relay the plan to Republican members of Congress at a closed-door lunch Tuesday.

“The administration urges Congress to provide $50.1 billion to deliver a truly world-class air traffic control network,” the letter said.

“I think the odds are quite high that there will be a meaningful investment in additional air traffic control technology improvements,” Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas, told reporters outside the Capitol before the closed-door meeting. Asked what he thought about the other $40 billion in the request, Mr. Cruz said only that “we’re focused on the safety investments.”

Mr. Duffy first voiced the demand for $50 billion Friday night during a news conference about a nationwide ground stop that led to air travel disruptions across the East Coast. Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion to modernize the country’s aging air traffic control system.

The F.A.A. had halted thousands of flights for hours because of communication interruptions between air traffic controllers and pilots. The problems began after a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark., Friday afternoon appeared to overload the system, and issues emerged with another router in Texas, federal officials said.

It was the third such ground stop in F.A.A. history.

item.title: I.R.S. Opens Criminal Probes as Part of Trump’s Pursuit of Left-Wing Groups
item.description:
The Internal Revenue Service has initiated at least four criminal investigations as part of the Trump administration’s crackdown on left-wing groups that began after the killing of Charlie Kirk last year, according to an internal agency memorandum viewed by The New York Times.

The pages of the memo viewed by The Times do not identify the subjects of the investigations, nor is their current status known. But even the existence of the criminal investigations is the clearest sign yet that President Trump has successfully dragged the typically technocratic I.R.S. into enforcing his political agenda.

The memo describes the work done by a group of a dozen I.R.S. officials detailed to a task force formed in response to Mr. Kirk’s death on Sept. 10, 2025. Mr. Trump ordered agencies across the government to investigate the antifascist movement, or antifa, and other groups that espouse “extremism on migration, race and gender,” among other views.

Under that order, the I.R.S. was told to investigate whether nonprofits were “directly or indirectly financing political violence or domestic terrorism.” In March, officials from the criminal investigations branch of the service began working with the task force out of the F.B.I. headquarters.

The I.R.S. work on the task force has also involved rapid response to events like protests at Delaney Hall, an immigrant detention center in Newark, N.J., the memo states. Protesters and Immigration and Customs Enforcement have repeatedly clashed at the site, and a Democratic member of Congress is among the people who have been charged with a crime after an encounter with federal agents there.

I.R.S. officials reviewed financial information, including subpoenaed Venmo records, about people arrested during those protests, as well as businesses that the officials believed could be funding them. At one point, I.R.S. officials used facial recognition and tattoo analysis databases to help identify individuals, the memo said.

Many nonprofits and their tax lawyers have feared that the I.R.S., with its vast stores of financial information and power to enforce tax law, could become a potent tool in the president’s vendetta against liberal organizations. That concern began last year, when Mr. Trump publicly called for the I.R.S. to strip elite universities and other nonprofits of their tax-exempt status, a move that would upend their finances.

But because audits and tax investigations are protected under federal taxpayer privacy law, it has been unclear to what extent the I.R.S. has heeded the Trump administration’s push to scrutinize left-leaning groups. The memo viewed by The Times is the first window into the work the I.R.S. has actually undertaken to carry out the demands from the White House.

The internal status report, circulated among leaders in I.R.S. Criminal Investigation, describes the activities of the I.R.S. team on the task force between March and July of this year. The Times viewed the first six pages of the eight-page memo and did not view its two-page appendix identifying the targets of the I.R.S. investigations. One focus for the group is investigating people who doxx or threaten government officials, the memo states.

A spokesman for the I.R.S. said the agency’s criminal branch “has collaborated with federal law enforcement agencies, including the F.B.I., to investigate individuals and entities that may be funding domestic terrorism or political violence.”

In addition to the four criminal investigations mentioned in the memo, the group of I.R.S. special agents and analysts have also referred at least four tax-exempt groups to the civil side of the agency that conducts audits, the memo said. The document said that the group of I.R.S. officials had been assigned to nine grand juries and helped the F.B.I. with financial analysis, including of whether groups had improperly filled out Form 990, the main tax form for nonprofits.

The Trump administration has cast its focus on “domestic terrorism” as a way to prevent political violence, but its enforcement campaign has only fueled fears about the federal government’s penalizing lawful political activity. In the days after Mr. Kirk’s killing, the Justice Department pushed U.S. attorneys to investigate George Soros’s Open Society foundation, a major donor to liberal causes.

And in the spring, the government charged the Southern Poverty Law Center, a nonprofit group that has long tracked hate groups, with defrauding its donors. Prosectors have charged Tyler Robinson, a 23-year-old man, with killing Mr. Kirk and have not accused him of working with any outside group.

Within the I.R.S., officials have discussed the creation of a new process for revoking the tax-exempt status of nonprofit groups, according to three people familiar with the change. Organizations that have been indicted or have had senior members of their leadership indicted would face an expedited audit, conducted in a matter of months, that could result in the loss of their tax-exempt status, the people said. But I.R.S. lawyers have raised concerns about the legal rigor of such a process, and the agency has so far not implemented it.

Beyond the Delaney Hall protests, the I.R.S. detail to the F.B.I. task force has also helped work on the federal law enforcement response to the shooting at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner in the spring, as well as a shooting at a mosque in San Diego in May. The I.R.S. group also assisted with the Ultimate Fighting Championship event that Mr. Trump hosted on the White House lawn in June, though its exact role is unclear.

But much of the memo viewed by The Times describes the bureaucratic challenges the I.R.S. officials have faced working with the F.B.I. The “continual turnover” of F.B.I. leadership on the task force and the bureau’s “culture of lack of information sharing” has made it difficult for the I.R.S. to establish itself in the task force, the memo stated. An F.B.I. spokesman did not respond to a request for comment.

The I.R.S. memo, which is unsigned, describes how, overall, opportunities for the group have been limited. Some potential financial crimes have been identified, the memo states, but they are not related to the task force’s work “because there was no specific threat directed at a government entity, its property or a government employee.” In some instances, other I.R.S. agents ignored emails from the task force or did not inform the group that they were already working a case, the memo said.

The I.R.S. group recommends that it be given a broader remit to focus more squarely on “investigating the misuse of 501(c)(3) organizations and/or individuals with nexus to terrorism,” referring to the tax code section that applies to many nonprofits. Under federal law, any organization that the federal government officially identifies as a terrorist group immediately loses its tax-exempt status.

With roughly 3,000 employees, the criminal investigation branch of the I.R.S. is a relatively small slice of the agency overall. But it has been frequently deployed as part of broader Trump administration initiatives. An inspector general report this year detailed the time I.R.S. criminal agents spent patrolling the streets of Washington and Memphis, Tenn., as part of the administration’s law enforcement efforts there. That came at the expense of work on criminal tax investigations, the inspector general found.

item.title: Man Indicted in Bomb Threat at Illinois Ethanol Plant
item.description:
A federal grand jury in Illinois indicted a man on Tuesday on charges of threatening to detonate an explosive device at a Peoria ethanol plant.

The man, Andrew Kozak, was charged with two felonies in connection with a bomb threat at the BioUrja Renewables ethanol plant that led to a lengthy evacuation in Peoria last week.

Emergency workers found and deactivated one device at the plant on Friday, though the charges against Mr. Kozak do not specifically accuse him of placing that device. Mr. Kozak was indicted on two felony counts — threats regarding explosives and interstate communications of a threat — which could carry years in prison if he is convicted.

A LinkedIn profile for an Andrew Kozak in the Peoria area listed him as an employee of BioUrja, where it said he had worked since February. Company officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Court records did not indicate whether Mr. Kozak had hired a lawyer. Officials at the federal public defender’s office in the Central District of Illinois did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The indictment was sparse on details but said that Mr. Kozak “sent an email to BioUrja which indicated that explosive devices had been placed” at the Peoria facility. Mr. Kozak was scheduled to make an initial court appearance in U.S. District Court in Peoria on Tuesday afternoon. The indictment did not describe a motive for the threats.

While crews searched the plant for more explosives on Friday and Saturday, events were canceled, roads were blocked, and residents within a one-mile radius of the plant were told to evacuate. The search for additional explosives concluded on Saturday without any being located, and residents were allowed to return home. No injuries were reported.

Ernesto Londoño and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Hegseth Nominates His Former Aide to Lead the Army
item.description:
After more than six months of delay, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to lead the Army.

Mr. Hegseth fired the Army’s previous chief of staff, Gen. Randy George, in April without explanation. That dismissal, along with the departure of Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll in August, has left the Army essentially rudderless as it struggles to adapt to the threat posed by cheap, deadly drones and missiles that have pounded U.S. bases in the Middle East.

General LaNeve, who previously worked as Mr. Hegseth’s senior military aide, is now serving dual roles as the Army’s acting chief of staff and its vice chief. Mr. Hegseth nominated Lt. Gen. Marcus S. Evans to serve as the vice chief of staff.

Their nominations were sent initially to the White House for President Trump’s approval. Earlier this week the White House forwarded the nominations to the Senate Armed Services Committee, congressional officials said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel moves.

“For 36 years, I’ve served in the U.S. Army, currently as the vice chief of staff,” General LaNeve said in a statement. “I’m deeply honored by the president’s trust and confidence for the nomination to serve as the chief of staff of the U.S. Army, and, if confirmed, I look forward to continuing to serve our soldiers, their families and our nation.”

In most cases, senior military leaders who are nominated to lead their services are easily confirmed by the Senate. But it is not clear that General LaNeve’s nomination can muster the necessary votes to advance, officials said.

General LaNeve was widely thought to be Mr. Hegseth’s top choice for the job, but the uncertainty surrounding support for his nomination has delayed the Pentagon from sending it forward. The Republican rout in the midterm elections could make General LaNeve’s confirmation even less likely next year.

Still, he must overcome serious doubts from G.O.P. lawmakers who are frustrated with the way Mr. Hegseth has led the Pentagon and who are reluctant to vote for senior officers with close ties to the secretary.

Senator Joni Ernst, an Iowa Republican who deployed to Iraq and served 22 years in the National Guard, has voiced repeated skepticism about General LaNeve. Earlier this year, she suggested three alternatives to the White House. Her top choice was Gen. Christopher T. Donahue, who was serving as the top Army officer in Europe before Mr. Hegseth forced him to retire, officials said.

Some lawmakers have quietly expressed hope that General Donahue could return to active duty if Mr. Hegseth were impeached or forced to resign. For now, though, Mr. Hegseth’s job seems safe.

Last week, House Republicans banded together to shelve an effort to impeach Mr. Hegseth, shielding him from a damaging rebuke and a potential ouster. Democrats have vowed to make another effort to impeach Mr. Hegseth in January when they will have a majority in Congress.

The next few weeks will be critical for Mr. Hegseth, who will be pushing lawmakers to approve as much as $350 billion in new defense spending. The Pentagon badly needs that money to continue paying for the war with Iran and Mr. Trump’s ambitious modernization program.

Mr. Hegseth’s decision to nominate General LaNeve, despite the doubts about his fitness for the Army chief job, suggests that Mr. Hegseth is not chastened by the looming threat of impeachment and plans to continue to fight for his and Mr. Trump’s priorities.

item.title: A Death Along Lake Superior Revives Memories of ‘the Gales of November’
item.description:
On the morning of Nov. 6, something was moving in the surf along the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

A man walking his dog along the beach looked more closely: It was a body.

Lake Superior had just given up its latest casualty.

The shores of the largest of the Great Lakes are scenic. They are also blustery, and the danger they pose to human life becomes pronounced during each year’s 11th month. Lake Superior’s shoreline communities commemorate the grim toll of shipwrecks and lives claimed by its waters, which become a cauldron of wild and deadly storms during the fall season, known in folklore — and a Gordon Lightfoot song — as “the gales of November.”

Winds barrel across the surface of Lake Superior at speeds that conjure the gusts of a hurricane. Waves two dozen feet high or more roll through open water, or crash over shoreline cliffs.

The body found near the shores of Harvey, Mich., was identified by the police as a 62-year-old man from Calumet, a village about 70 miles away. The man’s survivors requested that he not be identified. The Marquette Police Department, working from witness reports, believed he had been seized by the waves a day before when Superior’s powerful currents pounded Black Rocks, an outcropping of volcanic basalt where he had gone to take photographs.

Snatched from the surface, like too many before him, on decades of windy November days.

Lake Superior is the deepest of the Great Lakes, and is typically considered the largest body of freshwater in the world, with a surface area of more than 31,000 square miles. Depending on the season, its edges lap or pummel the shores of Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Ontario.

Its cliffs, forests and rugged shores are striking, and it is a major artery for the workhorses of maritime shipping that move cargo through interlocking waterways to the ocean and ports thousands of miles away.

But the tempests of Lake Superior have overtaken hundreds of ships. Its routes and shoreline points have earned reputations as maritime graveyards.

The lake earned its most fearsome legacy on Nov. 10, 1975, when a 729-foot freighter, the Edmund Fitzgerald, sank in a calamitous storm that was enshrined in Mr. Lightfoot’s ballad “The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald.”

Twenty-nine crew members and the ship vanished beneath the waves.

The tragedy has become a touchstone for lake communities every November, when the gales descend. The recent drowning death fell days before annual commemorations for the ship’s crew.

In Paradise, Mich., the Great Lakes Shipwreck Museum livestreamed a memorial for the descendants of the Fitzgerald’s crew.

In Detroit, the Rev. Todd Meyer of the Mariners’ Church pulled the rope on the church bell 29 times, once for each crew member.

“We have been doing this for 51 years,” he said.

In Minnesota, the fate of the 62-year-old man was incorporated into the ceremony for the ship’s crew at the Split Rock Lighthouse, where the names of the crew members were read aloud.

Hayes Scriven, the site manager of the lighthouse, said in a speech that the death, along with those from other shipwrecks and rescues, was “a sobering reminder of the power of the lake.”

“A lot of us around the lake, involved in the Fitz memorials, talk about how the Fitz crew itself can stand as a memorial for all of the people that are lost on Lake Superior and the Great Lakes,” he said in an interview.

The Marquette Fire Department called the latest drowning “a sad, harsh reminder of Lake Superior’s power.”

Its crosscurrents, massive waves and turbulent waters can render its name misleading, said the fire chief, Ian Davis.

“It is really not a lake,” Chief Davis said in an interview. “It is an inland sea.”

Lake Superior becomes “more of a tempest” when large, low-pressure systems form in October and November, said Ketzel Levens, a forecaster with the National Weather Service in Duluth, Minn.

The season is often described by meteorologists as unstable when the summer water temperature is warmer on average compared with the arrival of the cold air, she said.

Those factors “create these really, really strong winds,” Ms. Levens said. “And depending on what direction they are coming, they might run across Lake Superior for potentially hundreds of miles.”

Waves propelled to shallower depths rear up to break along the shore, sometimes swamping high cliffs.

“As tall as the wave is, it is about as deep,” she said.

On the day the Calumet man went missing, the lake had been living up to its seasonal reputation of battering winds and bullying waves.

The National Weather Service in Marquette had issued a gale warning. Winds picked up by 1 p.m., with a buoy registering waves of 15.5 feet, Ben Warren, a Weather Service meteorologist in Marquette, said.

Those waves were some of the highest recorded since Oct. 24, 2017, when they measured almost 30 feet, he said.

On that day, two friends, Robert Anderson, 53, and Sarah Hall, 37, went to Black Rocks to take photographs.

Like others before them and since, they were swept away.

Mr. Anderson’s body washed up about a month later in a nearby harbor.

Ms. Hall’s body has never been found.

Unruly conditions, including on the day of the latest death, can keep divers, helicopters and boats grounded.

Still, Capt. Ryan Grim, the police chief in Marquette, said witnesses told rescuers that some people tried to help the man who was claimed by the lake.

“They actually tried to throw a jacket out to him,” he said.
